Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

confirm verb

say or show that something is true

also assure, affirm, assert, bear out, can you confirm?

classical

Cic. Fam. 7.16.2: Balbus mihi cōnfirmāvit tē dīvitem futūrum
Cic. Att. 16.5.2: hoc cum mihi nōn modo cōnfirmāsset sed etiam persuāsisset

cōnfirmō, cōnfirmāre, cōnfirmāvī, cōnfirmātum

verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, or an accusative and infinitive, and a dative of the person assured · Conjugation on Wiktionary

assure, state as certain; bear out

To tell someone for certain, or to prove a point with arguments (cōnfirmāre … deinde contrāria refūtāre, Cic. de Or. 2.80). Its first sense is to make firm or strengthen, and of people, to encourage (see encourage); Lewis & Short.

Other words

  • affirmō, affirmāre, affirmāvī, affirmātum — assert, state positively

    verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, or an accusative and infinitive · also used · classical · Cic. Div. 2.8: nihil ut adfirmem, quaeram omnia · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    To state something firmly as one’s own claim, where cōnfirmō often assures someone else of it. Also written adfirmō.

  • comprobō, comprobāre, comprobāvī, comprobātum — confirm by facts, make good; approve

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Ter. And. 824: ut beneficium verbīs initum dūdum nunc rē comprobēs · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    To bear out by the event what was said; its commoner sense is to approve wholly of something (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Balbus mihi cōnfirmāvit tē dīvitem futūrum.

    Balbus assured me you’ll be rich.Cic. Fam. 7.16.2

  • hoc cum mihi nōn modo cōnfirmāsset sed etiam persuāsisset

    when he had not only assured me of this but convinced me of itCic. Att. 16.5.2

  • abs tē postulō atque ōrō Chreme ut beneficium verbīs initum dūdum nunc rē comprobēs

    I ask and beg you, Chremes, to make good now in fact the favour you began in words a while agoTer. And. 823–824

See also prove, convince, encourage, true.
